paragraphs: Image captioning requires deciding what an image contains and expressing that content in language. The paper argues that conventional sequential caption generators can introduce irrelevant meaning, produce limited variety, and generalize inadequately. It proposes separating the identification of semantic content from the construction of the sentence that describes it.

The method first extracts an explicit semantic representation of the image. It then builds a caption through a recursive, bottom-up composition process. Rather than treating caption construction solely as a sequence of successive outputs, this procedure organizes language through repeated composition. The explicit separation between meaning and syntax is intended to help preserve the image’s content during generation.

The paper reports that this compositional procedure requires less training data, generalizes better, and generates more diverse captions than conventional approaches. Its contribution is a different organization of the captioning task: an intermediate representation carries the visual meaning, while recursive construction handles its linguistic expression. The stated benefits connect that architectural separation to both semantic fidelity and learning efficiency.
neurips-2018-a-neural-compositional-para.tldr: Separating visual meaning from recursive sentence construction improves image captioning’s semantic fidelity, diversity, and data efficiency.

paragraphs: Extreme multi-label classification assigns a few relevant labels from a very large collection. Organizing those labels in a tree can make prediction manageable, but a tree method designed for choosing one class does not automatically handle several correct labels. This paper examines probabilistic label trees as a principled way to make that transition.

The authors show that probabilistic label trees generalize hierarchical softmax to the multi-label setting with a no-regret result for precision at k, which evaluates relevance among the top k predictions. They also prove that the common shortcut of selecting one label and treating the task as multi-class classification is not generally consistent. That result identifies a theoretical problem with an otherwise convenient reduction.

Their implementation, extremeText, performs significantly better than hierarchical softmax with that shortcut and XML-CNN in the reported comparisons. It is also competitive with several leading approaches in predictive performance, model size, and prediction time. Together, the theory and experiments support tree-based multi-label prediction that preserves the task’s multiple-label structure while remaining practical for online deployment.
neurips-2018-a-no-regret-generalization-.tldr: Probabilistic label trees provide a theoretically justified and efficient multi-label extension of hierarchical softmax.

paragraphs: When neural-network training is distributed across a cluster, synchronous updates can leave faster workers waiting for slower ones. These delayed workers, or stragglers, make the time spent waiting part of the training cost. Bayesian distributed stochastic gradient descent addresses this problem by deciding when to stop accepting gradient messages for an update.

The algorithm uses amortized inference in a deep generative model to jointly predict mini-batch gradient computation times for the particular cluster. Those predictions determine an optimal cutoff, beyond which messages from slow workers are ignored. The central idea is to use a learned account of worker performance to guide the cutoff rather than rely on a fixed threshold.

In the reported experiments, eagerly discarding straggler computations improves throughput and convergence measured against elapsed time by reducing idleness. Using predicted runtimes improves substantially over static-cutoff approaches and reduces neural-network training time on large clusters. The findings show that accepting fewer gradient messages can still accelerate training in practice when the avoided waiting time outweighs the cost of discarding them.
neurips-2018-bayesian-distributed-stocha.tldr: Predicting worker runtimes lets distributed training discard late gradients strategically and reduce elapsed training time.

paragraphs: Expectation Maximization is widely used to fit statistical models, but its usual guarantees do not ensure finding the best likelihood value. It can instead stop at an undesirable stationary point. This paper investigates whether adding parameters that are unnecessary for describing the data can nevertheless make that optimization problem easier.

The setting is mean estimation in Gaussian mixture models whose mixing weights are already known. The authors compare fixing those weights to their correct values with allowing EM to estimate them. This deliberately over-parameterized formulation gives the optimization procedure additional freedom, even though the extra parameters are statistically redundant.

For symmetric mixtures with two Gaussian components, the authors prove that estimating the weights allows EM to reach the global likelihood maximizer from almost any initialization of the means. Keeping the known weights fixed can fail frequently. Experiments on other Gaussian mixtures show similar behavior, extending the evidence beyond the proved case without making that broader observation a theorem. The result illustrates how additional parameters can improve optimization even when they provide no needed expansion of the statistical description.
neurips-2018-benefits-of-over-parameteri.tldr: Allowing EM to estimate already-known mixture weights can help it avoid bad optima, with a global guarantee for symmetric two-component Gaussian mixtures.

paragraphs: Mode collapse occurs when a generative adversarial network fails to represent much of the variety in its target distribution. BourGAN approaches this problem geometrically: different modes are treated as structure in a space where distances between data points can be measured. That structure guides the design of the generator’s latent inputs.

The method embeds a subsample of the dataset from an arbitrary metric space into Euclidean space while preserving the distribution of pairwise distances. The embedding determines the latent dimension automatically and supports construction of a Gaussian mixture from which latent vectors are sampled. Training combines this mixture with an additional term in the GAN objective.

The paper supplies theoretical analysis for every major step and evaluates the method on real and synthetic data. In those experiments, generated samples cover most modes while avoiding unwanted samples, and the method outperforms several recent GAN variants on multiple metrics. The contribution is to connect latent-space construction directly to the geometry of the data, rather than treating the source of latent randomness as independent of the mode-collapse problem.
neurips-2018-bourgan-generative-networks.tldr: BourGAN uses distance-preserving embeddings to construct a Gaussian-mixture latent space that improves empirical coverage of data modes.

paragraphs: Observational causal analysis often depends on controlling for confounders, but the measurements available for those confounders can be noisy. Adjusting for imperfect measurements can leave causal-effect estimates biased. This paper studies how a large collection of noisy measurements can help recover the underlying confounders and reduce measurement-induced bias.

The proposed framework uses matrix factorization to infer confounders from observed covariates before applying causal inference methods. It accommodates missing entries and different data types, making the preprocessing useful across a variety of causal estimators. The approach draws on the information shared across many measurements rather than treating each recorded covariate as an accurate confounder measurement.

The authors bound the error of the resulting average treatment effect estimator. In a linear regression setting, they prove consistency when preprocessing uses Exponential Family Matrix Completion. Numerical experiments with synthetic and real clinical data demonstrate the procedure’s effectiveness. These results support combining measurement recovery with causal estimation, while locating the stated consistency guarantee in the specific linear setting analyzed.
neurips-2018-causal-inference-with-noisy.tldr: Matrix factorization can recover confounder information from many noisy measurements and reduce bias in causal-effect estimation.

paragraphs: This paper studies linear regression when unusually large observations can occur in both the inputs and outputs. It evaluates predictions with absolute error rather than squared error. That choice makes the regression objective suitable for estimating a conditional median, shifting the target of prediction as well as the way errors are measured.

To handle heavy tails on both sides of the problem, the authors propose a truncated minimization objective. They establish an excess-risk bound of order square root of d divided by n, where d is the input dimension and n is the sample count. The guarantee holds with high probability without requiring exponential moment conditions on either inputs or outputs.

A second result distinguishes the case of bounded inputs. There, ordinary empirical risk minimization with absolute loss remains adequate even if the outputs are heavy-tailed. The findings therefore clarify when a modified objective is useful and when the classical procedure can suffice. Their main theoretical advance is obtaining strong probability guarantees while relaxing tail requirements that would exclude the distributions under consideration.
neurips-2018-ell-1-regression-with-heavy.tldr: A truncated absolute-loss regression objective provides high-probability risk guarantees without exponential moment assumptions on inputs or outputs.

paragraphs: A dataset may contain useful predictive information even when too few examples are available to train an accurate model. This paper asks whether that potential can be estimated before it can be realized. The target is the best performance available within a model class, rather than a fitted model that already achieves it.

For d-dimensional inputs with isotropic covariance and labels given by an arbitrary noisy function, the authors estimate the variance explainable by the best linear predictor using O(sqrt(d)) samples. They also obtain an O(sqrt(d)) sample result for estimating the best linear classifier’s prediction error. In the settings compared, learning any function correlated with the underlying model requires samples linear in d, even without label noise.

The approach is extended to unknown arbitrary covariance, including linear prediction after a nonlinear embedding. Experiments on synthetic and real data demonstrate practical viability. These findings suggest a role in choosing which features or datasets to collect when observations are expensive: estimating a feature set’s explanatory potential may require substantially less data than building a predictor that uses that potential.
neurips-2018-estimating-learnability-in-.tldr: The potential accuracy of a model class can sometimes be estimated with far fewer samples than are needed to learn a useful predictor.

paragraphs: Amortized inference learns to reuse work across many posterior-inference problems. It maps observations to approximate distributions over the quantities that generated them. Designing that mapping requires reversing the dependency structure of a generative model, and the paper argues that heuristic reversals can introduce incorrect independence assumptions that limit inference accuracy.

The authors introduce an algorithm for constructing a minimally faithful inverse of any generative model’s graphical structure. Faithfulness means that the inverse does not assert independencies absent from the original model. Minimality is expressed through a local maximum in the number of valid independencies encoded, retaining structural simplification without introducing false separations between variables.

The paper proves the algorithm’s correctness and reports better amortized inference than existing heuristic inversion approaches. The distinction matters because an approximation’s architecture can restrict what dependencies it is capable of representing, regardless of how it is trained. Constructing the inverse systematically addresses that structural source of error while preserving as many true independencies as the stated local optimality property permits.
neurips-2018-faithful-inversion-of-gener.tldr: A provably faithful inversion algorithm preserves the dependency structure needed for more accurate amortized inference.

paragraphs: Combining several views of a scene requires keeping track of which observations refer to the same physical locations. This paper introduces recurrent networks whose memory is a three-dimensional feature tensor, with a one-to-one correspondence between locations in the scene and locations in that memory. New views contribute to a shared spatial representation.

The network uses differentiable feature warping that accounts for the observer’s motion, together with learned depth-aware unprojection. These operations align features from an input image with the three-dimensional scene memory. Object detection, segmentation, and reconstruction are then performed directly from that accumulated memory, making the combined spatial representation the basis for recognition.

Experiments show substantially better generalization than geometry-unaware LSTM and GRU networks, particularly with multiple objects and objects blocking one another. Combined with active view selection, the model learns to seek informative viewpoints that help resolve those occlusions. The reported results connect explicit geometric organization with both integrating existing observations and deciding which additional observations would be useful.
neurips-2018-geometry-aware-recurrent-ne.tldr: A geometrically aligned three-dimensional memory improves multi-view recognition and supports choosing viewpoints that resolve occlusions.

paragraphs: After producing a clustering, a separate question remains: how confidently can its quality be assessed? This paper introduces the Sublevel Set method to obtain sufficient guarantees that a clustering is close to optimal and essentially unique. Here, uniqueness allows small perturbations, so the guarantee concerns approximate agreement rather than absolute identity.

The method applies to clustering loss functions that admit convex relaxations. To obtain its guarantees in practice, one solves a convex optimization problem. This creates a way to assess a proposed clustering through a related optimization problem with convex structure. Because the conditions are sufficient, they establish quality when satisfied without claiming that every good clustering must satisfy them.

The authors demonstrate the approach for K-means on realistic datasets, obtaining guarantees that do not depend on a specified data distribution. The contribution is a general framework for certifying clustering quality relative to a chosen objective. It addresses both how far the objective value might be from the optimum and whether substantially different solutions remain plausible under the method’s guarantee.
neurips-2018-how-to-tell-when-a-clusteri.tldr: The Sublevel Set method uses convex optimization to provide sufficient guarantees of clustering near-optimality and approximate uniqueness.

paragraphs: Pairwise preference aggregation tries to recover candidates’ underlying ratings from judgments comparing two candidates at a time. When judgments are sparse and noisy, the choice of which comparison to request becomes part of the problem. Hybrid-MST uses active sampling to direct the available testing budget toward informative pairs.

The method combines a Bayesian optimization framework with the Bradley-Terry preference model to construct a utility function and estimate each pair’s expected information gain. Gaussian-Hermite quadrature makes that estimation computationally efficient. The resulting information scores guide comparison selection, connecting the current uncertainty about ratings to the next data the procedure seeks.

At each trial, the strategy uses either the pair with globally maximal expected information gain or a minimum-spanning-tree sampling approach, with the choice determined by the test budget. Evaluations on simulated and real-world datasets show stronger preference aggregation than the compared state-of-the-art methods. The stated contribution is this budget-dependent combination of sampling strategies, supported by a probabilistic measure of how useful each comparison is expected to be.
neurips-2018-hybrid-mst-a-hybrid-active-.tldr: Hybrid-MST uses expected information gain and a budget-dependent sampling strategy to recover ratings from sparse, noisy pairwise preferences.

paragraphs: Binary classification does not always need to force an unambiguous label for every observation. Confidence-set learning instead constructs one set for each class, with a specified probability guarantee that the set covers that class. Where the two sets overlap, the procedure explicitly allows either label, representing ambiguity in the classification.

This paper proposes a support vector classifier for constructing those sets flexibly. The learning task must balance two goals: keeping each class’s non-coverage rate under control and making the ambiguous overlap small. Treating these goals together connects the reliability of the sets with how often the resulting classification can give a definite answer.

The authors prove that their learner can control non-coverage and minimize ambiguity with high probability. They also develop efficient algorithms and provide numerical evidence of effectiveness. The contribution is a direct support-vector approach to learning class-covering sets, with theoretical guarantees addressing both coverage and uncertainty. Its output makes ambiguity part of the prediction rule rather than requiring every observation to receive a single class.
neurips-2018-learning-confidence-sets-us.tldr: A support-vector method learns class confidence sets while controlling non-coverage and reducing ambiguous overlap with high probability.

paragraphs: Deep learning depends on efficient tensor operations, including matrix multiplication and high-dimensional convolution. Manually optimized libraries can provide that efficiency, but supporting new hardware requires substantial engineering effort. This paper proposes learning how to search for efficient operator implementations, reducing dependence on implementations tuned by hand for particular devices.

The framework learns statistical cost models specialized to the tensor-program domain. These models guide a search through billions of possible program variants, helping identify promising implementations within that large space. It also transfers models across workloads to accelerate the search, allowing knowledge acquired during one optimization task to assist another.

Experiments report performance competitive with state-of-the-art hand-tuned libraries on low-power CPUs, mobile GPUs, and server-class GPUs. The results support learned search as a practical route to efficient tensor operators across different hardware targets. The contribution concerns the implementation of the computation itself: learning helps choose how an operator runs, addressing the engineering burden that hardware-specific libraries place on deployment and broader system optimization.
neurips-2018-learning-to-optimize-tensor.tldr: Learned cost models guide tensor-program search to achieve performance competitive with hand-tuned libraries across several hardware types.

paragraphs: Neuronal population recordings contain many dimensions of activity. Targeted dimensionality reduction summarizes them using separate low-dimensional subspaces associated with experimental variables, such as a stimulus or an animal’s behavior. This paper gives that decomposition a probabilistic foundation, addressing ad hoc choices and limits in the flexibility or interpretation of earlier methods.

The proposed generative model represents low-dimensional structure through a low-rank factorization of linear regression. Inference combines Expectation Maximization with direct maximization of the marginal likelihood. The authors also develop an efficient procedure for estimating the dimension of each subspace, so the method addresses both the structure of a response and how many dimensions describe it.

On simulated data, the approach outperforms alternatives in parameter-estimation mean squared error and in recovering the correct encoding dimensionality. The paper also reports more accurate inference of activity subspaces than demixed PCA. These findings support using an explicit probabilistic model to separate task-related patterns of neural activity and estimate their complexity, rather than choosing the low-dimensional summary solely through a less structured procedure.
neurips-2018-model-based-targeted-dimens.tldr: A probabilistic low-rank regression model more accurately estimates task-related neural subspaces and their dimensions in the reported comparisons.

paragraphs: A system can benefit from exploring uncertain options even when each individual user prefers the option with the best current average reward. This paper studies that conflict in a bandit problem with a succession of short-term players. The controller offers payments to encourage exploration while seeking high total reward and low total compensation.

The authors derive a compensation lower bound involving the time horizon, each arm’s expected reward gap, and the Kullback-Leibler divergence between its reward distribution and that of the best arm. The bound connects the cost of incentives with both the reward difference and the statistical distinguishability of alternatives. It formalizes a cost that ordinary reward-focused bandit analysis does not directly capture.

They then analyze three algorithms and show that each achieves logarithmic growth in both regret and compensation, matching the stated lower-bound scaling in the horizon. Experiments illustrate the algorithms’ behavior. The results show that, in this known-compensation setting, incentives can support exploration while keeping both the accumulated reward shortfall and the required payments controlled.
neurips-2018-multi-armed-bandits-with-co.tldr: Three compensated bandit algorithms achieve logarithmic regret and compensation while incentivizing greedy short-term players to explore.

paragraphs: Adversarial interference with state information can cause a deep reinforcement learning agent to learn or choose poor behavior. This paper proposes Meta-Learned Advantage Hierarchy, a framework that addresses attacks through the agent’s decision process. It is designed to work without specifying a particular attack model and to mitigate bias introduced during learning.

The framework learns separate nominal and adversarial sub-policies online. A supervisory master agent uses the sub-policies’ advantage functions to detect the presence of an adversary and guide learning. This hierarchical organization gives the system distinct policies for the two conditions and a learned mechanism for recognizing adversarial interference.

The paper provides algorithm analysis and simulations in OpenAI Gym environments. It reports significantly lower learning bias than the compared state-of-the-art policy-learning approaches, including under heavy attacks on state information. The findings support handling robustness within online policy learning itself. The reported advantage concerns reduced bias under the evaluated attacks; the framework’s independence from a specified attack model describes its design rather than a guarantee of success against every possible adversary.
neurips-2018-online-robust-policy-learni.tldr: An online hierarchy of nominal and adversarial sub-policies reduces learning bias under the evaluated state-information attacks.

paragraphs: Policy regret evaluates learning while accounting for how an adversary would react to different learner actions. External regret does not account for those reactions in the same way. The paper first shows that these objectives can conflict in online learning: there are settings where performing well under either measure forces poor performance under the other.

The authors then study repeated games in which the opponent is self-interested. Here, the conflict disappears in the stated results, and a broad class of algorithms can ensure both regret properties when the opponent also uses an algorithm from that class. The condition on the other player is central to this algorithmic guarantee.

The paper also introduces policy equilibrium and proves that play generated by no-policy-regret algorithms converges to it. Coarse correlated equilibria form a strict subset of these policy equilibria. Accordingly, in the game-theoretic setting described, no external regret implies no policy regret, but the reverse implication fails. This separates the two equilibrium requirements while explaining why compatible learning behavior is possible in games despite the earlier incompatibility result.
neurips-2018-policy-regret-in-repeated-g.tldr: Policy and external regret can conflict in online learning, but repeated games admit compatible guarantees and a broader notion of policy equilibrium.

paragraphs: Explaining a neural-network prediction can involve identifying training examples that help account for it. This paper proposes representer points: training points associated with a particular test prediction through a mathematical decomposition. The goal is to make the connection between an output and the examples involved in learning its parameters explicit.

The authors show that a network’s pre-activation prediction can be expressed as a linear combination of training-point activations. The coefficients, called representer values, indicate the importance of those points. Their signs add another layer of explanation: positive values identify excitatory points, while negative values identify inhibitory points, distinguishing contributions that support the prediction from those that oppose it.

This signed interpretation provides more information than an undifferentiated measure of training-point importance. The paper also reports substantially greater scalability than influence-function methods, allowing real-time feedback. Its contribution combines a decomposition of the prediction with an example-based explanation format: a user can inspect relevant training points together with the direction of their contribution to the network’s pre-activation output.
neurips-2018-representer-point-selection.tldr: Representer points explain a network’s pre-activation prediction through signed contributions from training examples.

paragraphs: Communicating an objective to a reinforcement learning agent can be difficult when it requires writing a reward function by hand. This paper combines two forms of human guidance: expert demonstrations and preferences between trajectories. Both are used to learn what behavior should be rewarded, giving the agent an objective derived from human input.

A deep neural network models the reward function from those demonstrations and preferences. Its predicted rewards then train a DQN-based reinforcement learning agent. This separates learning the objective from learning how to act: the reward model interprets the human guidance, and the agent optimizes behavior using that model’s outputs.

Across nine Atari games, the approach beats the imitation-learning baseline in seven and achieves strictly superhuman performance in two. The authors also examine how well the reward model fits, investigate reward hacking, and study noise in human labels. These additional analyses matter because success depends on the learned reward expressing the intended objective. The results demonstrate the potential of combining demonstrations and preferences while also examining failures in that communication process.
neurips-2018-reward-learning-from-human-.tldr: Combining demonstrations and trajectory preferences to learn rewards beats imitation learning in seven of nine Atari games.

paragraphs: Many learning objectives depend on spectral functions of matrices, including log-determinants and nuclear norms. Computing their gradients generally has cubic complexity, making repeated full-gradient updates expensive. Stochastic gradients could reduce that burden, but constructing an unbiased estimate for these matrix-dependent functions is itself a substantial obstacle.

The paper develops unbiased stochastic gradients for spectral sums, an important subclass of spectral functions. Its construction combines randomized trace estimation with randomly truncated Chebyshev expansions. Choosing how to truncate the expansion is part of the method: the authors design truncation distributions with a variance-optimality property, addressing the variability that affects stochastic optimization’s speed and stability.

The resulting gradient estimators are used to build stochastic optimization methods for objectives containing spectral sums, and the authors rigorously analyze their convergence rates. Numerical experiments demonstrate their utility. The contribution therefore connects an estimator construction to a usable optimization procedure, tackling both the absence of straightforward unbiased gradients and the need to control their variance without routinely computing a full spectral gradient.
neurips-2018-stochastic-chebyshev-gradie.tldr: Randomized trace estimation and stochastic Chebyshev truncation yield unbiased gradients for optimizing spectral-sum objectives.

paragraphs: Stochastic composite mirror descent is a family of scalable optimization methods that can use a problem’s geometry and composite structure. This paper analyzes its behavior for convex and strongly convex objectives with non-smooth losses. For both cases, it establishes high-probability convergence rates that are optimal apart from a logarithmic factor.

The authors then apply the optimization-error bounds to the generalization of multi-pass stochastic gradient descent in a nonparametric setting. Their bounds depend only logarithmically on the number of passes, provided the step sizes are square-summable, meaning that the sum of their squares is finite. This condition is part of the stated result, rather than an unrestricted guarantee for repeated training.

The logarithmic dependence improves on existing expectation bounds with polynomial dependence on the number of passes. It provides theoretical support for multi-pass SGD’s ability to avoid overfitting under the analyzed conditions. The analysis also removes bounded-subgradient assumptions often used in earlier work, and numerical results support the theoretical findings. Together, these advances strengthen both optimization and generalization guarantees.
neurips-2018-stochastic-composite-mirror.tldr: High-probability mirror-descent bounds yield improved multi-pass SGD generalization guarantees when the step-size sequence is square-summable.

paragraphs: Removing small neural-network weights can reduce storage and arithmetic, but irregularly scattered removals are difficult for CPUs and GPUs to exploit efficiently. Pruning larger structured groups improves hardware utilization, yet can require retaining more weights to preserve accuracy. TETRIS aims to combine the sparsity of individual-weight pruning with the practicality of structured pruning.

The method reorders input and output dimensions so that small weights, initially scattered through the network, become concentrated in structured groups. Those groups can then be pruned. The tile-matching analogy describes this rearrangement: changing how weights are organized creates groups that are better suited to removal and hardware execution.

The reported results achieve sparsity comparable to irregular element-wise pruning with negligible accuracy loss. GPU experiments also show speedup proportional to sparsity. These are empirical findings from the evaluated settings, connecting the organization of removed weights with actual execution gains. The contribution is an approach to the accuracy-efficiency tradeoff that coordinates the pruning algorithm with the structured work that computing hardware can use effectively.
neurips-2018-tetris-tile-matching-the-tr.tldr: TETRIS rearranges small weights into structured groups, achieving high sparsity and proportional GPU speedups in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning seeks to use unlabeled data to reduce the need for labeled examples. This paper studies that possibility through mixture models without imposing parametric distributional assumptions. Its assumptions instead describe the mismatch between a mixture learned from unlabeled data and the true mixture associated with the unknown class-conditional distributions.

Under those assumptions, the authors establish a labeled-sample complexity lower bound of order K log K, where K is the number of classes. Their broader results suggest that near-optimal classification can be possible with few labels in nonparametric settings. For more than two classes, a central challenge is learning the permutation that associates mixture components with class identities.

The paper controls the resulting classifier’s error using Wasserstein distance between mixing measures and provides finite-sample results for excess risk. It also develops three estimation algorithms through a connection to bipartite graph matching. Experiments illustrate an advantage of maximum likelihood over majority vote. The work links mixture quality, component-to-class assignment, and labeled-data requirements within one analysis of multiclass semi-supervised learning.
neurips-2018-the-sample-complexity-of-se.tldr: The paper relates multiclass semi-supervised learning’s label requirements to mixture mismatch and the challenge of assigning components to classes.

paragraphs: Graph embeddings turn nodes into vectors while preserving relationships from a graph. Their quality often depends on manually chosen settings, such as random-walk length, that need adjustment for each graph. This paper replaces previously fixed choices with parameters learned through backpropagation, allowing the graph representation’s construction to adapt to the task.

The method places attention over the power series of the graph’s transition matrix, guiding the random walk toward the training objective. Its attention parameters act on the data-generation process used to learn embeddings and are not needed during inference. This makes attention a way to learn which graph relationships training should emphasize.

On link-prediction tasks across social, collaboration, and biological networks, the method improves on state-of-the-art results, with reported error reductions reaching 20–40%. Learned attention differs substantially between graphs and corresponds to optimal hyperparameter choices found by manual tuning of existing methods. The findings support adapting the walk-based training information to each graph instead of expecting one fixed configuration to preserve all graph structures equally well.
neurips-2018-watch-your-step-learning-no.tldr: Learning attention over random-walk structure improves node embeddings while removing some manual graph-specific tuning.
